Pelagic thresher sharks (Alopias pelagicus) are born at a precaudal length of 82 centimeters [Lb = 82 centimeters], during which the yolk sac is completely resorbed by the time the total length reaches approximately 12 to 40 cm. This rapid reliance on endogenous yolk reserves sustains the developing embryo throughout gestation, and the relatively large size at birth is consistent with the K-selected life history strategy observed across most lamniform sharks. Newborn individuals are fully independent from the moment of parturition, possessing the elongated caudal fin that characterizes the species and which is employed as a hunting tool to stun schooling prey. The precaudal length at birth is a critical metric for understanding neonatal survivorship, as larger pups generally face lower predation risk and can begin foraging immediately. Field surveys in the eastern Pacific have confirmed that neonates typically emerge during the warmer summer months, coinciding with peaks in prey abundance. This timing may enhance early growth rates and reduce the period of highest vulnerability during the first few months of life. The transition from yolk dependency to active hunting is abrupt, and the initial feeding events are thought to target small pelagic fishes and squid that are abundant in the same epipelagic waters inhabited by adult conspecifics.

Males of this species attain sexual maturity upon reaching a precaudal length of approximately 142.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 142.5 centimeters], corresponding to a total length range of 267 to 276 cm. For females, puberty occurs at a somewhat larger precaudal length of 147.5 centimeters [Lp = 147.5 centimeters], with a total length spanning 282 to 292 cm. This sexual dimorphism in size at maturation is common among Alopiidae and likely reflects the greater energetic demands of gestation and parturition that females must accommodate. The reproductive cycle is characterized by a low fecundity, with females producing a single litter of 2 pups [N_R_i = single litter of 2 pups] every two years [F_R_i =  every two years]. This exceptionally slow reproductive rate is among the lowest recorded for any shark species and renders Alopias pelagicus highly susceptible to population depletion under fishing pressure. The interval between successive pupping events is thought to be linked to the energetic cost of vitellogenesis and the protracted gestation period, which together impose a significant recovery time before the female can again become gravid. Estimates derived from captive observations and field sampling indicate that these reproductive parameters are stable across the species range when measured at the typical seawater temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C].

Under ambient oceanic conditions of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], the oldest documented individuals of Alopias pelagicus have been estimated to live for approximately 38.5 years [am = approximately 38.5 years] based on vertebral banding patterns, a longevity that aligns with the slow life history typical of large oceanic sharks. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a similarly protracted juvenile period, with males requiring approximately 7.5 years [tp = approximately 7.5 years] from birth to reach puber at a temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C]ty. Females, which mature at a larger size and later age, take approximately 8.6 years [tp = approximately 8.6 years] from birth to attain reproductive maturi at a temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C]ty. The delay in female maturation is a common feature among elasmobranchs and is thought to be driven by the need to achieve a body size sufficient to support the energetic costs of pregnancy and the production of relatively large pups. Age estimates derived from growth rings in the vertebral centra have been validated through mark-recapture studies and bomb radiocarbon dating, providing confidence in these longevity and maturation time frames. The combination of a long prereproductive period and low fecundity underscores the limited capacity of this species to recover from even moderate levels of exploitation.

The ultimate precaudal length recorded for female Alopias pelagicus is 187 centimeters [Li = 187 centimeters], while males reach a smaller maximum precaudal length of 168 centimeters [Li = 168 centimeters]. This size differential is reflected in the corresponding ultimate wet weights, with females attaining an adult body mass of approximately 137,300 grams [Wwi = approximately 137,300 grams] and males reaching a maximum wet weight of about 98,500 grams [Wwi = about 98,500 grams]. These asymptotic sizes are achieved after many years of sustained growth following the onset of maturity and are consistent with the allometric scaling relationships derived from length-mass regressions in this species. At the point of sexual puberty, female pelagic threshers weigh approximately 73,900 grams [Wwp = approximately 73,900 grams], whereas males at the same developmental stage have a wet weight of around 64,600 grams [Wwp = around 64,600 grams]. The divergence in mass between the sexes during maturation mirrors the differences in length and is likely a consequence of the higher metabolic demands placed on females during reproduction. Comparative studies among alopiid sharks indicate that Alopias pelagicus occupies an intermediate position in terms of both maximum length and mass, being smaller than the common thresher but larger than the bigeye thresher.

Neonates in this species are born at an age of approximately 1.8 years [ab = approximately 1.8 years] when measured at the stable ambient water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C] characteristic of their subtropical and tropical habitat. This extended developmental window is among the longest gestation periods recorded for any elasmobranch and is thought to facilitate the production of large, well-developed pups that are immediately capable of independent foraging. The yolk-sac placenta that nourishes the embryo throughout gestation ensures a continuous supply of nutrients, and the resorption of the yolk sac is completed by the time the embryo reaches a total length of 12 to 40 cm, well before parturition. The slow pace of embryonic development relative to other oceanic sharks may be a consequence of the relatively stable thermal environment and the energetic trade-offs associated with producing a small litter of large offspring. Compared to other alopiid sharks, the maximum lifespan of 38.5 years [am = 38.5 years] at 26.7 °C is relatively long, a pattern typical of oceanic species with low natural mortality at a temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C]. This life history configuration, characterized by delayed maturity, low fecundity, and substantial maternal investment, renders the pelagic thresher particularly vulnerable to overfishing and slow to recover from population declines, reinforcing the need for stringent conservation measures across its global range.

Pelagic threshers inhabit the epipelagic zone of tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide, where they are most frequently encountered in waters between the surface and a depth of 150 meters. Their distinctive elongated caudal fin, which can equal the length of the rest of the body, is used as a whip to stun and capture schooling prey such as anchovies, sardines, mackerel, and squid. This specialized hunting strategy is energetically costly but highly effective, allowing individuals to subdue multiple prey items in a single strike. Tagging studies have revealed that Alopias pelagicus exhibits a diel vertical migration pattern, ascending to the surface at night to feed and descending to deeper waters during the day, likely to avoid visual predators and to follow the movements of their prey. The species is frequently caught as bycatch in longline and gillnet fisheries targeting tuna and swordfish, and its low intrinsic rate of population increase makes it one of the most vulnerable elasmobranchs to anthropogenic mortality. Conservation measures including time-area closures and the adoption of circle hooks have been proposed to reduce incidental capture and improve the survival prospects of released individuals.
